title: NAS 410 Audit Documentation for Phoenix Suppliers
description: NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 audit evidence for Phoenix engine, rotorcraft and repair-station NDT programs, ready for your Level 3 to sign. Contact Atlantis.
h1: NAS 410 and Nadcap Audit Documentation for Phoenix-Area Engine, Rotorcraft and Repair Station NDT Programs
html:
Engine and APU component makers, rotorcraft and defense subcontractors, and the many FAA repair stations across the Valley of the Sun share one recurring headache: proving to an auditor that every NDT technician, procedure and examination is controlled the way NAS 410 and Nadcap AC7114 require. Atlantis NDT assembles and reviews that audit evidence for the Phoenix area, and your company's Responsible Level 3 signs it. If an audit is on your calendar, tell us which one and which methods; we reply within one business day.

Where the line sits between Atlantis and your own program

We want this clear before anything else. Atlantis does not serve as anyone's Responsible Level 3, does not certify technicians to NAS 410, and offers no NAS 410 training or examination service. Certification is an act of your company, done under the written practice your company owns. Approval of procedures, technique sheets, examinations and the written practice itself rests with the Level 3 your management designated in writing. Our part is ASNT NDT Level III consulting on the paperwork and the evidence: finding the gaps, drafting corrections in your format, organizing the records an auditor will sample, and rehearsing the audit with your people.

Two practical limits follow from that. Our Level III credentials cover UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, not eddy current, so eddy current technique content in your program is approved by a Level 3 certified in that method. And because Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, any help with an RT line is limited to reviewing procedures, technique charts and records as a Level III.

Engines, rotorcraft and space hardware: the Valley's aerospace mix

Greater Phoenix carries an unusual blend of aerospace work for one metro area. Honeywell Aerospace is headquartered in Phoenix and makes propulsion engines and auxiliary power units, which draws a ring of machining, coating, heat-treating and inspection suppliers into turbine-class work. In Mesa, Boeing builds and remanufactures the U.S. Army's Apache helicopters. MD Helicopters is headquartered in Phoenix and builds several helicopter models in the state, and Robertson Fuel Systems fabricates aircraft fuel tanks in Tempe.

The space and defense side is just as dense. Northrop Grumman produces satellites in the Phoenix area and, through the former Orbital ATK operations, makes launch vehicles and armament systems at sites in Chandler, Gilbert and Mesa. General Dynamics Mission Systems works on communications and satellite technology in Scottsdale, and the Arizona Commerce Authority lists avionics production in Phoenix among the state's strengths. A short drive down Interstate 10, Raytheon's missile business is headquartered in Tucson. Behind all of these sits a supplier base the state tracks at more than 1,250 companies.

For an NDT program, that mix means very different hardware passing through the same Valley shops in a single week: nickel and titanium rotating parts, steel gears and shafts, aluminum and composite airframe details, pressure-bearing propulsion components and space structures. Each product family carries its own customer specification, and the written practice has to cover all of them without contradicting any.

A state full of repair stations, and two rulebooks in one hangar

Arizona counts roughly 140 FAA-certificated maintenance operations, and its aviation maintenance workforce has ranked among the largest in the country. For a Part 145 repair station, NDT personnel requirements arrive from two directions at once. The FAA oversees the repair station manual and the training program, and FAA guidance acknowledges that the United States has no national certifying agency for NDI personnel, so qualification is employer-based. Meanwhile the maintenance data the station works to, and the airlines and OEMs it works for, frequently expect NAS 410 or an equivalent written practice.

The result is a common audit failure mode in the Valley: a repair station manual that says one thing about NDT qualification, a written practice that says another, and personnel files that follow neither completely. We map the three against each other, show where the manual must point to the written practice rather than repeat it, and draft the wording so that the FAA inspector, a customer auditor and a Nadcap auditor all read the same rule. Our aviation NDT consulting page covers the repair-station side of this in more detail.

Desert heat and the process control log

Valley summers create an audit issue that shops in cooler regions rarely meet. Penetrant and magnetic particle specifications set temperature limits for the part, the materials and in some cases the wash water, and a booth that sits comfortably inside those limits in January can drift outside them on a July afternoon if the building cooling struggles or parts arrive hot from machining or an outdoor staging area. Auditors in Arizona know this and look for evidence that someone measured and recorded the temperatures the procedure names, on the days it mattered.

The fix is mostly documentary. The procedure should say which temperatures are checked, how often, with which calibrated instrument and what happens when a reading falls outside the band, and the log form should have a place to record each one. Water heaters, chillers and dryers that affect the process belong on the calibration or verification register too. We review the logs for seasonal gaps, compare them against the procedure and specification, and redesign the forms so the record matches the requirement. Our equipment calibration guide describes how to keep the instruments in that register from lapsing.

Engine and APU hardware: what auditors press on

Turbine-related suppliers face some of the most detailed NDT audits in aerospace, and the paperwork has to match that detail.

  • Fluorescent penetrant. Sensitivity level, penetrant type and removal method must match what each customer specification calls out for each part family, and the process control log has to show the checks ASTM E1417 and the customer require, at the frequencies the procedure states. An auditor will compare a part's routing sheet with the line's settings on the day it was inspected.
  • Eddy current on rotating parts. Bolt-hole and surface techniques depend on reference standards, probe and instrument settings that must be fixed in an approved technique. Your eddy current Level 3 approves these; we help organize the record set and check that it is traceable.
  • Ultrasonic inspection of forgings and bar. Immersion techniques, reference blocks, scan plans and acceptance classes tied to ultrasonic specifications such as AMS 2630 need written technique sheets and examination specimens that reflect the product forms technicians actually inspect.
  • Magnetic particle on steel components. Gears, shafts and fittings bring ASTM E1444 checks on bath concentration, field strength indicators, lighting and demagnetization into the log review.

The common thread is traceability: from part number to technique, from technique to approval, from approval to the certified person who ran the job. Where one of those links depends on memory instead of a record, the auditor writes it up. See aerospace NDT compliance for the requirement-by-requirement view.

Rotorcraft and defense programs in the East Valley

NAS 410 has military roots: it took over from MIL-STD-410 on defense contracts in the late 1990s, and many defense purchase orders still invoke it directly. Suppliers to the helicopter, missile and launch-vehicle programs in Mesa, Chandler and Gilbert therefore meet NAS 410 both through Nadcap and through the contract itself, with government quality oversight layered on top. Three documentation issues come up again and again in that work.

First, retention. Defense programs run for decades, and a record retention clause written for commercial work may fall short of what the contract demands, so the written practice and the records procedure need to state the longer period where it applies. Second, controlled technical data. Specific examinations and technique sheets often reference drawings and specifications that fall under ITAR, so the way examination banks are stored, copied and shared has to respect those controls. Third, examiner and instructor qualification. Program reviews often ask who wrote and graded each examination and on what authority, and a file that shows only a grade fails that question.

Examination records: the file Valley auditors open early

NAS 410 requires general, specific and practical examinations in each method at each level. An auditor will usually pick two or three certified technicians and ask to see all three for each method they hold, then follow the trail back to the question bank and the practical specimens. Weak spots we see in Arizona files include specific examinations that test a generic body of knowledge instead of the procedures and specifications the person uses, practical specimens with no documented flaw map, missing evidence that the examiner was qualified to administer the test, and regrades with no record of why a score changed.

We audit the examination files against the written practice and the standard, then prepare corrected templates: a specific-examination blueprint tied to the documents each technician works to, a practical-specimen register with flaw records, and an examination cover sheet that captures examiner, date, grade and approval in one place. The examinations themselves, and their administration, remain your program's. The AC7114 examination records page and training records and certificates describe the evidence in more depth.

The record set we prepare for your Level 3's signature

  • Written practice review and redline against NAS 410 and, where European customers apply, EN 4179, with every customer flow-down noted beside the clause it affects.
  • Responsible Level 3 designation file: the appointment letter, the methods that person holds, and the documented arrangement for methods they do not.
  • Personnel record packs for each certified technician: training against approved outlines, experience logs, the three examinations, vision results, certification and recertification records.
  • Outside agency file: agreements with any training provider or examiner you use, named in the written practice and controlled by your Level 3.
  • Procedure and technique register showing approval, revision and the specification each document satisfies.
  • Process control and calibration registers for penetrant and magnetic particle lines, ultrasonic and eddy current instruments, light meters and reference standards.

Each item comes back marked for approval rather than issued, because issuing it is your company's act. For the written practice itself, written practice development for aerospace explains how we structure one.

Revision 6 timing for Arizona shops

NAS 410 Revision 6, released by AIA with Accuris in December 2025, adds Appendix D, a scheme that lets a Level 2 earn credit for defined NDT tasks and, once the thresholds in each category are met, sit the initial Level 3 examination; AIA also says the edition makes the certification rules clearer. For a repair station or engine supplier with experienced Level 2s, the points route only helps if activity records exist to support it, so it is worth deciding early whether your written practice will use it. We draft an activity log format that a Level 3 can verify, alongside the redline of your written practice against the new revision. Read NAS 410 explained for a fuller account, and work from the purchased standard for the exact wording. Repair stations should also check whether the airlines and engine makers they work for have said anything about Revision 6, because a customer letter can set the effective date for your shop regardless of what the standard allows.

How we deliver the work in the Phoenix area

Most of the document work happens remotely: you share files or screen time, we return redlines, record packs and registers. For export-controlled material we agree the handling route before any file leaves your network. The on-site part is the mock audit, where we walk your penetrant line, inspection booths and record room with your team, pull personnel files at random, and observe a technician running a job against its approved technique, the way a Nadcap auditor would. If the real audit produces nonconformances, we help with root-cause analysis and with the objective evidence the task group needs before closure; NDT audit consulting explains that follow-through.

Scoping a first engagement takes the written practice, a roster showing every certified technician and the methods and levels each holds, your Nadcap slash sheets or customer audit checklist, and the last audit report with responses. If certification due dates are tracked in a spreadsheet that keeps slipping, our expired technician certifications guide shows a cleaner way to keep them current.

Related Atlantis services in Arizona

Atlantis also provides NDT consulting in Phoenix for non-aerospace programs, aerospace NDT consulting in Tucson for suppliers further south, and NDT training for Phoenix employers built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. That course work follows the ASNT document; under NAS 410 your Responsible Level 3 decides whether any outside hours count. The national overview is at NAS 410 audit compliance documentation, and Nadcap AC7114 audit readiness covers the audit itself.

faq.q: Our repair station manual and our written practice disagree about NDT qualification. Which one wins?
faq.a: The FAA holds you to the repair station manual, and your customers hold you to the written practice they accepted, so the honest answer is that both must agree. The usual fix is for the manual to reference the written practice for NDT personnel rules rather than restate them. We draft that alignment for your accountable manager and Responsible Level 3 to approve.

faq.q: Can Atlantis sign our eddy current technique sheets?
faq.a: No. Our Level III certifications are in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Eddy current techniques are approved by a Level 3 certified in eddy current, normally your own. We can still organize the eddy current records, check traceability and prepare the files for that person's review.

faq.q: Is Atlantis able to give our technicians their NAS 410 examinations?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not administer NAS 410 examinations, deliver NAS 410 training or certify anyone to NAS 410. We review your examination files, build compliant templates and blueprints, and help your program's own examiners and Responsible Level 3 keep the records audit-ready.

faq.q: We supply Apache and missile programs. Does NAS 410 apply even without Nadcap?
faq.a: Often yes, because many defense contracts invoke NAS 410 directly. Read the purchase order and its quality clauses, then make sure the written practice states which revision applies to which program, along with any longer retention period the contract requires.

faq.q: How do we handle ITAR-controlled technique sheets during a consultant's review?
faq.a: Tell us before sharing anything. The controlled files can then be examined at your facility, or shown to us over a meeting link your IT team hosts, so the data never sits on an outside server. Unrestricted documents such as the written practice can usually be shared normally.

faq.q: Do we need separate written practices for Honeywell-type engine work and airframe work?
faq.a: Usually not. One written practice can cover several product families if it states each customer's additional requirements clearly, often in an appendix or a flow-down matrix. Separate documents tend to drift apart and confuse auditors.

faq.q: What does a mock audit in our Phoenix-area facility involve?
faq.a: A walk of the AC7114 checklist and your slash sheets with your team, random pulls of personnel files, a look at process control logs and calibration records, and observation of a technician running a real job against its technique. You receive a findings list ranked by audit risk.

faq.q: Will the NAS 410 Revision 6 points route help our Level 2s reach Level 3?
faq.a: It can, if your written practice adopts it and you keep activity records a Level 3 can verify. Without records made at the time of the work, the points cannot be supported at audit. Check the purchased standard and your customers' expectations before adopting it.

faq.q: Can we use Atlantis's SNT-TC-1A training toward NAS 410 certification?
faq.a: Atlantis's courses follow ASNT SNT-TC-1A and are not NAS 410 training. Under NAS 410, your Responsible Level 3 decides whether any outside training hours can be credited, and records that decision in line with the written practice.
